values.conflict_note: The ingested statute snapshot says 25% for 2023; the Department of Revenue's 2023 form and its credit percentage table both say 50%. The agency value is used. Same cause as the 2024 conflict: the snapshot omits a later amendment, which has not been ingested. Until 2026-11-11 this repository recorded 25% from the snapshot alone.

sources.quote: The credit was 50% of the federal EITC amount for Tax Years 2024 and 2025, but will be reduced to 25% in Tax Year 2026.

values.conflict_note: The ingested statute snapshot says 38% for 2024; the Department of Revenue publishes 50%. The agency value is used. The snapshot's heading mentions a 'trigger' that its text does not contain, so it predates or omits the amendment that set 50%. That amendment has not been ingested.

sources.quote: The credit was 50% of the federal EITC amount for Tax Years 2024 and 2025, but will be reduced to 25% in Tax Year 2026.

values.conflict_note: The ingested statute snapshot says 25% for 2025; the Department of Revenue publishes 50%. The agency value is used. Same cause as the 2024 conflict.

sources.quote: The credit was 50% of the federal EITC amount for Tax Years 2024 and 2025, but will be reduced to 25% in Tax Year 2026.

values.conflict_note: The ingested statute snapshot says 20% for 2026 and later; the Department of Revenue publishes 25% for 2026. The agency value is used. Same cause as the 2024 conflict.

gaps: No value is recorded for tax years from 2027, so the engine refuses to compute the credit for 2027 onward. The Department of Revenue's credit percentage table (https://tax.colorado.gov/income-tax-topics-earned-income-tax-credit, read 2026-11-11) has a row '2026 and later 25%'. It is not recorded as a 2027 value because the statute snapshot is known to be out of date, the amending act (HB24-1134) has not been read, and a secondary source (PolicyEngine) notes the percentage can rise with state revenue.
